result:
A thousand words is not very many. It's a long letter, a short story that hasn't earned its ending, the inventory of a small apartment. It's about four minutes of speech at a normal pace, less if you're nervous. When people say *a picture is worth a thousand words*, I think they mean that a picture arrives all at once and words have to file in single-file, and by the time the last ones show up the first ones have gotten bored and wandered off.

So let me spend them on something.

Here is what I keep noticing: the enormous amount of the world that exists only in the plural, and only briefly. Not species or continents — those get their own documentaries. I mean the specific arrangement of three coats on a hook by a door, the middle one still holding the shape of a shoulder. I mean the particular grayish color that a mug of tea goes when you've forgotten it for ninety minutes and the milk has surrendered. Nobody is keeping these. They happen and they resolve and the room moves on. There must be, at any given moment, some staggering number of these small configurations — the way the light lands on a countertop at 4:15 in November in a kitchen in Rotterdam, the exact tilt of a bicycle against a wall in Lima — and almost all of them go unwitnessed, or witnessed only distractedly, by someone thinking about something else.

I find I don't experience this as a tragedy. It seems more like the basic generosity of the arrangement. The world isn't rationing its interesting moments to the observant; it's producing them wildly, indiscriminately, at a rate that makes attention feel less like a duty and more like helping yourself at a very large buffet where the food keeps being replaced.

Attention is the whole thing, though, isn't it. There's a well-known idea that attention is a form of love, or prayer, or at least the precondition for either. I believe some version of this but I want to complicate it, because attention can also be predatory — the attention of the hunter, the auditor, the person scanning a room for someone more important to talk to. What distinguishes the loving kind isn't intensity. A hunter is extremely attentive. The difference is something about the direction of the interest: whether you're looking in order to *take* something from what you see, or looking because the thing seems like it might be more than you assumed, and you want to find out.

I think this is why boredom is so often a moral failure disguised as a mood. Not always — exhaustion is real, and some rooms genuinely have nothing in them. But a great deal of what passes for boredom is a decision, made preemptively and then defended, that a thing has been fully accounted for. The commute. The meeting. The neighbor's story about her hip. Once you've decided something is fully accounted for you've built a small wall and then complained about the view.

I once read that the medieval monks had a word for the specific noonday listlessness that came over them in the middle of a long day of prayer: *acedia*. It got classified as a sin, which sounds harsh, until you realize what they were actually naming. Not tiredness. A kind of refusal. The sense that nothing further is worth doing, that the day has been used up, that the next hour is merely the previous hour again. What made it a sin, I think, was the implicit claim it made about reality — that reality had run out. The monks were in the business of insisting it hadn't.

There's a related thing I keep circling, which is the strange status of the second time. First times get all the credit. First kiss, first snow, first apartment, and there's a whole industry of advice about staying open to novelty, seeking the new, beginner's mind. But almost everything good in a life is a *repetition*. The person you love is someone you have seen thousands of times. The song that undoes you undoes you on the fortieth listen. Skill is entirely made of repetition; so is comfort, so is trust, so is home. The novelty cult has the arithmetic backwards. What you want is not more first times but the capacity to have a fortieth time that isn't dead — to reread the poem and find the line you'd been reading past.

This is harder than novelty-seeking and much less photogenic. It doesn't require a plane ticket. It requires believing that the thing in front of you has depth you haven't reached, which is an act of faith about ordinary objects and ordinary people, and which is frequently wrong. Sometimes you go back to the poem and it really was as thin as you thought. Sometimes the neighbor's story about her hip is just a story about her hip. But the alternative — assuming exhaustion in advance — guarantees you'll be right, in the way that closing your eyes guarantees you'll see nothing.

I notice I've been writing about attention for several hundred words and haven't paid attention to anything. Let me fix that, or gesture at fixing it.

A word: *sillage*. It's French, and it means the wake a ship leaves, and it also means the trail of scent a person leaves in a room after they've walked through it. One word for both. Someone decided that the disturbance a hull makes in water and the way you can tell your grandmother was just here are the same phenomenon, and they were right, and now I can't stop seeing it. Everything leaves a sillage. Conversations do. Bad moods do — you can walk into a kitchen and know an argument happened in it. The word exists because someone was paying the loving kind of attention to something invisible and then handed it to the rest of us.

That's what I'd want to do with a thousand words, or with any number: hand something over. Not a conclusion. A noticing, with the noticing still warm.

The coats on the hook. The tea gone gray. The wake behind the boat and the ghost of a perfume in an empty room, filed under the same heading by someone long dead who was, for a moment, awake.

Nine hundred and eighty-something. Close enough.
